feat: support kimi-k3 tool call style (#806)

# feat: support kimi-k3 tool call style

Kimi-K3 replaces the Kimi-K2 tool-call markers with a nested,
token-delimited block format. This adds a `kimi_k3` builtin structural
tag and a `kimi_k3_xml` JSON-schema style for it.

## Output format

An assistant turn (line breaks added for readability; blocks are emitted
back to back):

```
<|open|>think<|sep|>reasoning...<|close|>think<|sep|>
<|open|>response<|sep|>text...<|close|>response<|sep|>
<|open|>tools<|sep|>
  <|open|>call tool="str_replace_editor" index="1"<|sep|>
    <|open|>argument key="command" type="string"<|sep|>str_replace<|close|>argument<|sep|>
    <|open|>argument key="path" type="string"<|sep|>/app/dummy<|close|>argument<|sep|>
  <|close|>call<|sep|>
  <|open|>call tool="read" index="2"<|sep|><|close|>call<|sep|>
<|close|>tools<|sep|>
<|close|>message<|sep|>
```

The generation prompt already ends with the first block's opening marker
(`<|open|>think<|sep|>`, or `<|open|>response<|sep|>` when thinking is
off), so the constrained output starts *inside* that block and the
grammar does not include that marker.

## What is supported

- **Message structure**: think block (reasoning mode only), mandatory
response block, optional tools section, closing
`<|close|>message<|sep|>`.
- **Tool calls**: multiple parallel calls concatenated with no
separator; calls with zero arguments; `tool_choice` = `auto` /
`required` / `forced`.
- **Arguments** (`style="kimi_k3_xml"`): one tag per argument. String
values are raw text; other types are JSON. Works with `any_order` and
`max_whitespace_cnt`.
- **`type` attribute is pinned to the declared property's schema type**,
because the vLLM parser uses it as a decoding switch (`type="string"`
keeps raw text, anything else is JSON-decoded). A mismatch would
silently change the decoded argument's type. `integer` and `number`
schemas both render as `number`, mirroring the model's `_xtml_type`;
keys with no declared schema (free-form / `anyOf` / mixed enum) keep the
full type set.
- **Key attribute escaping** (`&` → `&`, `"` → `"`), matching
the encoder's `_escape_attr_value` and the parser's reverse mapping.
Without it a property name containing `"` truncates the attribute and
the key is lost.
- **Termination**: the grammar ends at `<|close|>message<|sep|>`, so
`[EOS]` is masked until the message is closed and allowed right after.

## Implementation notes

- `FormatPropertyKey` / `FormatProperty` now take the property's
`SchemaSpecPtr` so a format can encode the value's type next to the key.
The JSON format ignores it; `XMLToolCallingConverter` is the only
subclass.
- Type deduction only runs for `kimi_k3_xml`; other XML styles are
unchanged.

## Testing

- Unit tests for the message shape, parallel / no-argument calls, tool
choices, reasoning on/off, type pinning and mismatch rejection, key
escaping.
- Converter tests for `style="kimi_k3_xml"`.
- Chat-template alignment: 16 generated cases (thinking on/off x 0/1/2
tools x auto/forced/required x single/parallel calls) validated against
outputs rendered by the official chat template.

fix(json_schema): make prefixItems entries positional per Draft 2020-12 (#834)

## Root Cause
`GenerateArray` built the prefix as `Sequence(prefix_elements)`, forcing
**every** `prefixItems` entry to appear. Per JSON Schema Draft 2020-12,
`prefixItems` entries are positional — an instance may validly end after
any prefix position (subject to `minItems`) — so arrays shorter than the
prefix were wrongly rejected (`[]` and `["a"]` for a two-item prefix),
and with a naive optional-chain fix the additional-items tail could
absorb prefix positions (issue #824).

## Fix
Build the array content as an **alternation of the full prefix (plus the
additional tail) and every shorter truncation**, keeping the first
`min(minItems, n)` entries mandatory:

```
content = full_prefix (+ additional tail)*
        | truncation ending at each position in [min(minItems, n), n)
```

Additional items are only reachable after the **complete** prefix, so a
mismatch inside the prefix range can never be rescued by the
additional-items path. Truncations are plain sequences (no
optional-chain backtracking), which keeps the grammar unambiguous.

## Test
- 3 new regression tests in
`tests/python/test_json_schema_converter.py`:
- `test_prefix_items_truncated_prefix_accepted`: the issue's accept-set
matrix (1111 for `[]`, `["a"]`, `["a",1]`, `["a",1,true]` with `items:
{}`), using the discriminating empty/one-element fixtures.
- `test_prefix_items_min_items_forces_prefix_head`: `minItems` still
forces the head of the prefix.
- `test_prefix_items_no_additional_items_allows_shorter`: `items: false`
forbids elements beyond the prefix but must not force the full length.
- Updated 3 existing tests that pinned the old behavior
(`test_non_strict`, `test_array_schema` additionalItems/unevaluatedItems
cases, `test_array_schema_min_max`): shorter prefixes now accepted,
wrong-position values still rejected.

[fix]: reject NUL characters in regex instead of crashing (#850)

This PR is mainly for solving the bug of a regex whose first byte is NUL
segfaults `Grammar.from_regex`. A NUL in any later position silently
truncates the pattern instead.

Major consumers already added their own Python-level NUL guard because
this crash cannot be caught downstream previously:

- vLLM — https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51796
- SGLang — https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34679

Those remain useful while older xgrammar releases are pinned, but they
only cover the paths each project routes through `regex`. Fixing it here
removes the need for the workaround and covers every entry point —
including a JSON schema's `pattern`, which reaches the same converter.

```python
python3 -c 'import xgrammar; xgrammar.Grammar.from_regex(chr(0))'   # SIGSEGV
```

Because it is a signal rather than an exception, a caller cannot catch
it: in a serving stack a single request carrying such a regex takes the
whole process down.

## Root cause

`RegexConverter`'s constructor guards on `std::string::empty()` but then
hands `regex_.c_str()` to `ParseUTF8`, which stops at the first NUL.
Those are different predicates:

```cpp
if (!regex.empty()) {                                    // std::string is non-empty
  regex_codepoints_ = ParseUTF8(regex_.c_str(), false);  // ...but c_str() is empty
  if (regex_codepoints_[0] == kInvalidUTF8) {            // empty vector -> OOB read
```

- **Leading NUL** — `c_str()` is `""`, `ParseUTF8` returns an empty
vector, and `regex_codepoints_[0]` reads past the end. SIGSEGV.
- **Later NUL** — `c_str()` is truncated, so only the prefix is compiled
into the grammar. No crash, no warning, wrong result.

`ParseUTF8` has no length-aware overload, so the C string is the only
thing it can key on.

This is the same family as #409, which fixed the empty-regex crash by
adding the `!regex.empty()` guard — that guard checks the `std::string`,
not the C string.

## Fix

Reject a NUL in the constructor, before `ParseUTF8`.
`XGRAMMAR_LOG(FATAL)` surfaces in Python as an ordinary `RuntimeError`,
the same path an unbalanced `[` already takes, so callers can handle it.
This closes the silent-truncation case too.

Considered instead: making `ParseUTF8` length-aware so a NUL becomes a
literal codepoint. That is a larger change to a shared utility, and it
gives NUL a meaning a regex does not need. Happy to go that way if you
prefer.

## Tests

`tests/python/test_regex_converter.py::test_null_character` — four
cases, two leading NUL (the crash) and two non-leading (the truncation),
so the check cannot later be narrowed to `startswith()`.

Built and run on aarch64:

- 4/4 new cases pass.
- **70 existing tests in that file still pass** (12 skipped:
`hf_token_required`).
- Reached through a serving stack, an unmodified SGLang goes from a dead
server to a clean HTTP 400 with the fix applied to xgrammar alone.

Fix segfaults from invalid arguments, corrupted serialized data and worker-thread errors (#869)

## Summary

Hardens the C++ boundary so that invalid arguments, corrupted or
incomplete serialized data, and errors raised on worker threads surface
as Python exceptions instead of crashing the process. Every fix comes
with a subprocess-verified reproducer turned into a regression test.

### Out-of-range arguments to the public API

- `apply_token_bitmask_inplace(..., indices=[...])`: validate every
index against both the logits and the bitmask batch size
(`ApplyTokenBitmaskInplaceCPU` only checked the no-indices path, so an
out-of-range index wrote through a wild pointer).
- `TokenizerInfo(vocab, vocab_size=N)` with `N < len(vocab)`: reject in
the constructor (`token_id_to_sorted_vocab_index_` was allocated with
`vocab_size` and written with real token ids).
- `accept_token(padding_id)`: padding ids pass the range check because
it uses the padded vocab size, but the special-token warning indexed
`decoded_vocab` with them; only decode ids backed by a real token.
- `traverse_draft_tree`: validate that every `retrieve_next_token` /
`retrieve_next_sibling` value is in `[-1, num_nodes)` and that the edges
form a tree (root has no incoming edge, every other node at most one).
Out-of-range values recursed into arbitrary memory; cycles or shared
nodes recursed without bound.
- EBNF macro arguments: nested tuples in `ParseMacroValue` bypassed
`nest_layer_guard_`, so `Token((((...` overflowed the stack.
- Token ids written in `Token(...)`, `ExcludeToken(...)` and token tag
dispatch must exist in the vocabulary. They are used as indices into
per-token arrays on compiler worker threads, so they are checked on the
calling thread before compilation starts (and skipped defensively on the
worker path).
- `GrammarMatcher(override_stop_tokens=[...])`: every id must be in `[0,
vocab_size)`; the ids are written into the token bitmask.

### Integer truncation and unbounded recursion in the grammar front-ends

- JSON schema `minLength` / `maxLength` / `minItems` / `minContains` /
`maxItems` beyond int32 were truncated when converted to repetition
bounds; a negative upper bound made `LegacyHandleRepetitionRange` call
`back()` on an empty vector. Maxima beyond int32 are now unbounded,
minima beyond it are rejected, and `ExpandRepetitionRange` checks its
range.
- The Lark parser had no nesting limit for groups; it now stops at 200
levels (each level uses a few KB of stack; the limit leaves a wide
margin below the 1 MB main-thread stack on Windows).
- Structural tag formats are limited to 100 nesting levels; the global
recursion limit is far deeper than the native stack allows for the
passes over the format tree.
- `picojson::parse` recurses once per nesting level with no limit. All
call sites go through `ParseJSON` (`cpp/support/json_parse.h`), which
parses with a picojson context that counts every nested array or object
in a `RecursionGuard`, so the maximum recursion depth applies while
parsing and a too-deep input is reported as a JSON parse error.
- `GrammarBuilder::AddGrammarExpr` checks that the grammar expr data
stays addressable by int32 offsets (reachable with a huge `indent`).
- The `xgrammar.testing` FSM helpers check `per_rule_fsms` before
indexing it.

### Deserialization of corrupted or incomplete data

The reflection-based deserializer restored CSR arrays, ids and bitsets
verbatim and never re-ran the invariants that the constructors
guarantee, so corrupted JSON crashed on first use (`root_rule_id`,
`grammar_expr_indptr`, FSM edges, mask indices, ...). It also never
rebuilt `token_id_to_sorted_vocab_index_`, so compiling any grammar with
token edges against a *legitimately* deserialized `TokenizerInfo`
segfaulted.

- `AutoDeserializeJSONValue` now calls `std::optional<std::string>
Validate() const` on reflection-based types that define it, after all
members are deserialized, and reports the message as a
`DeserializeFormatError`. `Validate()` is implemented for
`Compact2DArray`, `CompactFSM::Impl`, the `CompactFSMWithStartEnd`
serialization helper, `Grammar::Impl` and `TokenizerInfo::Impl`.
- `DynamicBitset` deserialization checks the array length before reading
the words.
- `CompiledGrammar` deserialization propagates the errors of its
`grammar` and `adaptive_token_mask_cache` sub-objects (they were
ignored) and checks that every mask matches the tokenizer.
- `TokenizerInfo::DeserializeJSON` rebuilds
`token_id_to_sorted_vocab_index_`.

The serialization format is unchanged.

### Errors on worker threads

`ThreadPool::Execute` tasks that threw (a terminated matcher or an
out-of-range index in
`BatchGrammarMatcher.batch_fill_next_token_bitmask`, or any check
failing during multi-threaded compilation) escaped the worker thread and
called `std::terminate`. The pool now records the first exception and
rethrows it from `Wait()` / `Join()` on the calling thread.

fix: memoize Cohere parameter wrappers for recursive references (#890)

`cohere_xml` crashes with a stack overflow when a union refers back to
itself through `$ref`, for example `V = anyOf[string, $ref V]`, mutually
recursive definitions, or recursion through a nested dict property or
list item. `FormatCohereParam` resolved the reference and expanded every
union option again on each visit, and options that are not themselves

on the parameter name, so `$ref` schemas get one memoized suffix rule
per URI, registered before the reference is resolved. A reference that
leads back to the same URI, directly or through nested dict/list items,
reuses that rule, and shared acyclic reference graphs are built once.

Bugfix: improve DeepSeek V4.1 tool-call performance and grammar correctness (#900)

This follow-up improves DeepSeek V4.1 Flash tool-call decoding in the
C++ compiler and matcher, including applications that construct and
serialize their own structural tags. It reduces token-mask traversal
overhead and fixes three correctness issues exposed by user-defined tool
schemas and exclusion patterns.

## Changes

1. **Skip rejected vocabulary subtrees when filling token masks.** Once
a subtree is known to be rejected, accepted-list and bitset masks still
scan its remaining uncertain tokens individually. Advance past them with
a bounded binary search. Preserve the per-token bookkeeping required by
rejected-list masks and multi-state unions.

2. **Render root object `const` and `enum` values as XML parameters.**
For example, `{"const":{"city":"Paris"}}` currently produces a bare JSON
object where the tool-call format requires a `city` parameter tag. Route
root object literals through the parameter formatter, preserving exact
fields and values, including empty objects. Object and array constants
inside parameters retain their existing fixed JSON serialization.

3. **Keep cached rules separate for each output encoding.** A `$ref`
reused by a raw string parameter and a nested JSON string can reuse the
wrong rule, rejecting valid output or accepting malformed JSON depending
on traversal order. Key both schema and reference caches by root
parameter-list, parameter-value, or nested-JSON context. Handle
recursive `$ref: "#"` consistently and preserve Cohere's recursive
tagged-value format.

4. **Honor exclusions hidden inside longer trie patterns.** With
`excludes=["abc", "xabcq"]`, the automaton can incorrectly accept
`xabcr`, even though it contains `abc`. Propagate excluded states
through failure links before removing incoming transitions. This fixes
the shared `AnyText`/`TagDispatch` behavior, including UTF-8 patterns
and token masks, without adding states or imposing an FSM size limit.
Exclusions remain scoped to free text; dispatched bodies and enclosing
tag delimiters keep their existing behavior.

## Validation

- After rebasing onto `main` at `e571161`, 2,759 Python tests and 74 C++
tests passed; 140 tests requiring Hugging Face access were deselected.
Formatting checks passed.
- Replayed the rebased revision `b6e197c` against the pre-rebase
results: all 53 schema-case records matched, and all 36,857 positions
across the 11 representative cases had identical token IDs and
full-vocabulary masks, with matching state-operation checks. This rebase
verification did not collect latency measurements.
- Added regressions for root object literals, mixed-context and
recursive references, overlapping exclusions, token masks, and dispatch
boundaries. Additional checks cover all three mask storage types,
multi-state unions, rejected tokens, forks, and rollback.
- Replayed custom serialized structural tags with the DeepSeek V4.1
Flash tokenizer and official encoder/decoder. The targeted schema matrix
passes 51 of 53 cases. Two valid encoder outputs remain rejected because
nested object/array constants retain fixed compact JSON serialization;
equivalent compact single-call and multi-call controls pass. This PR
retains that existing JSON literal restriction.

## Performance

The measurements below were collected before the rebase onto `e571161`:
they compare `main` at `ec67a61` with the combined changes at `0ef0830`,
not the rebased revision `b6e197c`. The run used an Apple M4 Pro (macOS
arm64, Release build), custom serialized structural tags, and
`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` tokenizer.

The two benchmark families use the full structural-tag grammar
definitions below. These generate the same compiler inputs used for the
measurements, including the DSML wrapper and whitespace settings.

<details>
<summary>Grammar definitions and replay inputs: integer array and
union</summary>

```python
import json
import xgrammar as xgr


def closed_object(properties):
    return {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": properties,
        "required": list(properties),
        "additionalProperties": False,
    }


# Case 1: the same grammar is used for both array lengths.
array_schema = closed_object({
    "v": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "integer"}},
})


# Case 2: N distinct object alternatives under anyOf.
def union_schema(n):
    return closed_object({
        "v": {"anyOf": [
            closed_object({
                "kind": {"const": f"k{i}"},
                "text": {"type": "string"},
            })
            for i in range(n)
        ]},
    })


def tool_grammar(schema):
    return {
        "type": "structural_tag",
        "format": {
            "type": "tag",
            "begin": "\n\n<｜DSML｜ calls>\n",
            "content": {
                "type": "tags_with_separator",
                "tags": [{
                    "type": "tag",
                    "begin": '<｜DSML｜ invoke name="run">\n',
                    "content": {
                        "type": "json_schema",
                        "json_schema": schema,
                        "style": "deepseek_v4_1_xml",
                        "any_order": False,
                        "max_whitespace_cnt": 4,
                    },
                    "end": "</｜DSML｜ invoke>\n",
                }],
                "separator": "",
                "at_least_one": True,
                "stop_after_first": False,
            },
            "end": "</｜DSML｜ calls>",
        },
    }


def compile_case(tokenizer_info, schema):
    compiler = xgr.GrammarCompiler(
        tokenizer_info, cache_enabled=False, max_threads=8,
    )
    wire = json.dumps(tool_grammar(schema), ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))
    return compiler.compile_structural_tag(wire)


# For these cases, this matches the pinned official encoder's completion.
def replay_text(arguments):
    return (
        '\n\n<｜DSML｜ calls>\n<｜DSML｜ invoke name="run">\n'
        '<｜DSML｜ parameter name="v" string="false">'
        + json.dumps(arguments["v"], ensure_ascii=False)
        + '</｜DSML｜ parameter>\n</｜DSML｜ invoke>\n</｜DSML｜ calls>'
    )


# (case name, tool-argument schema, arguments replayed through one `run` call)
benchmark_cases = [
    ("array_1024", array_schema, {"v": list(range(1024))}),
    ("array_8192", array_schema, {"v": list(range(8192))}),
    ("union_64", union_schema(64), {"v": {"kind": "k63", "text": "hello"}}),
```

fix: Mask overridden stop tokens until grammar completion (#905)

## Description

When using JSON mode with GLM-5.3 through vLLM, an overridden EOS token
can be allowed by the token mask inside an unfinished JSON string, but
rejected by accept_token(), causing an FSM failure

I found that the main cause is in `SetTokenBitmask`, where the

fix: enforce state limits in ToDFA and Intersect (#906)

Extracted from #901 by @izhuhaoran. This is the first piece of that PR
split into independently reviewable units. The branch keeps the original
commit and a revert of it at the bottom for attribution, so the net diff
against `main` is the last commit only (`cpp/fsm.cc`,
`tests/cpp/test_fsm.cc`).

`FSMWithStartEnd::ToDFA(max_num_states)` only rejected an input that
already had more than `max_num_states` states. The subset construction
itself was never bounded, so a small NFA could still expand into an
arbitrarily large DFA and the budget was effectively a no-op.
`Intersect(lhs, rhs, max_result_num_states)` had two related gaps: it
determinized both operands with `ToDFA()`, i.e. the default limit of
1000 states rather than the budget it was given, and it never bounded
the product automaton either.

## Changes

- `ToDFA`: check the DFA state count before every new closure is
inserted (character-range, rule-ref, repeat-ref, token and exclude-token
edges) and return an error once it reaches `max_num_states`.
- `Intersect`: pass `max_result_num_states` through to both `ToDFA`
calls, and return an error once the product automaton reaches the limit.

For callers this means a budget is now actually enforced (an error
instead of unbounded construction), and intersecting automata with more
than 1000 states works when the caller allows it. `Not` and
`MinimizeDFA` go through `ToDFA` and pick up the same bound. Nothing on
`main` outside the tests reaches these functions today; the
string-exclusion feature in #901 is the first production caller and
needs the larger budget for strings with `maxLength` of roughly 1000 or
more.

Warn when pattern is combined with minLength/maxLength in string schemas (silently dropped today) (#896)

Fixes #895 (stopgap; see "Scope" below)

## What

When a string schema has `pattern` together with
`minLength`/`maxLength`, `GenerateString` returns early on the pattern
branch, so the length-constraint branch is unreachable and **both length
constraints are silently dropped** (details + repro in #895).

This PR emits a warning when that combination is compiled, so
integrators notice the dropped constraints instead of silently losing
the schema's length bounds.

## Scope

This is a stopgap: the warning makes the dropped constraints observable,
but the constraint is still not enforced. A complete fix needs the
pattern automaton intersected with the length bound (automata product in
the FSM framework) — happy to work on that with maintainer guidance if
this direction is wanted.

## Testing

- Verified manually on xgrammar 0.2.3/0.2.7 + GPT-2: compiling
`{"type":"string","pattern":"^[a-z]+$","maxLength":3}` with this patch
logs the warning; the mask behavior is unchanged (matches #895's repro:
a 16-letter token is admitted at `value == "abc"`, producing a string
that violates `maxLength`).
- No behavior change for schemas without the combination; warning only
(no error), consistent with `WarnUnsupportedKeywords` style.

fix: preserve Unicode character class ranges (#909)

Extracted from #901 by @izhuhaoran, second piece after #906. The branch
keeps the original commit and its revert at the bottom for attribution;
the net diff against `main` is the `fix(fsm): preserve Unicode character
class ranges` commit. Same change as the closed #904, rebased.

Character-class FSMs mishandled Unicode in three places:

- Negated classes truncated codepoint endpoints to bytes, complemented
over an ASCII bitset, and then accepted every multi-byte sequence.
`[^\u0000-\U0010FFFF]` accepted all non-ASCII characters and non-ASCII
endpoints were dropped with a "clamping to 127" warning (#848).
- Positive ranges crossing UTF-8 widths were encoded in one packed-byte
call, which admits overlong encodings such as `C0 80`.
- The three-byte upper-tail path used lower bound `0x80` instead of
`0x8080`, so `[一-龥]` rejected every character with lead byte `E9` (`道`,
`部`, `金`, ...).

Fix: complement negated classes in codepoint space, split every range at
the UTF-8 width boundaries so only canonical encodings are accepted, and
fix the tail bound.

FSM snapshots grow because canonical UTF-8 needs more states. The
`hf_token_required` token-mask goldens change in two ways, verified by
diffing per-position masks against `main`: JSON string positions reject
exactly 5 more single-byte tokens (`C0 C1 F5 F6 F7`), and the
`[a-zа-я一-龥]+` test accepts 78 more CJK tokens that the tail bug had
rejected. Nothing else changes.

Overlaps #849, which fixes only the negated-class complement and still
admits overlong encodings. Closes #848.

Validation: 11 new regression tests that all fail on `main`;
`xgrammar_test` 77/77; full `tests/python` with `HF_TOKEN` 4764 passed.
Performance was measured in #904 on this same diff: a few percent more
compile time and mask latency on JSON, +12.6% mask latency on a
1024-char bounded Kimi XML string, from the extra states. This is a
correctness trade-off.

fix: start-state merging in MergeEquivalentStates and nested unbounded repetitions (#911)

Two correctness bugs in the grammar compilation pipeline, both reachable
from ordinary EBNF, regex and JSON-schema input on `main`. They were
found by diffing the regular-grammar flattener from #901 against
`GrammarMatcher`; the flattener was right both times and the matcher
side was wrong.

## 1. `MergeEquivalentStates` merges the start state away
(over-acceptance)

The "equivalent successor" rule merges two states that have the same
single predecessor, the same incoming labels and the same end-ness. When
the start state's only incoming edge is its own self-loop, it passes
that test, and a state reached from the start state by the loop label
looks equivalent to it. But the start state is also entered without
taking any edge, so the merged automaton accepts input that never
consumed the looped class. Three-state automata escape only because of
the `NumStates() < 4` early return.

- `root ::= [a-z]* [a-z] "c" "d"` accepts `cd`; `root ::= [a-z]* [a-z]
[0-9] [0-9]` accepts `12`.
- JSON schema `{"type": "string", "pattern": "^a*acd$"}` accepts `"cd"`,
through the regex FSM builder.

Fix: skip the start state in that rule, as candidate and as sibling. The
"equivalent precursor" rule is unaffected, since states with identical
outgoing edges have the same future however they are entered.

## 2. Nested unbounded repetitions reject everything (under-acceptance)

`RepetitionRangeExpander` inlines a single-element rule into the
repetition that references it, but copied the element verbatim instead
of visiting it. For `root ::= b{1,2}`, `b ::= a{2,}` the inlined
`a{2,-1}` was therefore never expanded into recursion, an unbounded
`kRepeat` edge reached the parser, and the parser's `repeat_count >=
Upper()` check against `-1` never let it enter the repeated rule.

- Regex `(a{2,}){1,2}`, `(a{2,}){2}`, `(a{1,}){1,2}` and the EBNF form
above reject every input.

Fix: visit the inlined element (`VisitExpr`) so nested repetitions go
through the expander like any other.

## Validation

- New tests:
`XGrammarFSMTest.MergeEquivalentStatesKeepsStartStateSeparate`
(hand-built four-state NFA),
`test_character_class_star_followed_by_same_class` (EBNF and
schema-pattern paths), and
`test_bounded_repetition_of_unbounded_repetition` (four regex cases plus
the EBNF form). All fail before their fix.
- `xgrammar_test` 78/78. Full `tests/python` with `HF_TOKEN`: 4851
passed, 3 skipped, 0 failed.
- No output change for unaffected grammars: the per-rule FSMs of the
builtin JSON grammar, several JSON schemas (bounded strings, patterns,
formats, numbers), Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 structural tags are
byte-for-byte identical before and after, and the full serialized
compiled grammar of a 1024-char bounded string schema (23.5 MB including
the token mask cache) is identical as well. So no goldens change.
- 600 random character-class grammars and a set of nested-repetition
regexes (`((a{2,}){1,2}){1,2}`, `(a{2,}b{1,}){1,3}`, `(a{130,}){1,2}`)
agree with Python's `re`.
- Performance: A/B against the unfixed `main` build on the same host,
alternating rounds. Compile time and mask latency for the builtin JSON
grammar, a 1024-char bounded string, an email regex, a schema `pattern`,
300 bounded strings, 400 properties with `max_whitespace_cnt` and large
repetitions are all within run-to-run noise; the compiled artifacts
being identical, the fixes add only a per-state comparison in the merge
pass and one visitor dispatch per inlined element.

`Grammar::FromRegex` sends some patterns through `RegexToEBNF` and
produces a small CFG with sub-rules instead of a single FSM.
`JSONSchemaFormat.excludes` (#901) needs an FSM for every string
constraint so it can intersect it with the exclusion automaton, so it
needs a way to flatten that CFG back.

the regular subset `RegexToEBNF` emits without re-parsing its terminals:
byte strings and character classes go through the existing FSM builders.
Each finite rule call is inlined with private entry and exit states, so
one call cannot return into another call's continuation, and a direct
tail self-reference loops back to that call's own entry. Bounded
repetitions are unrolled, unbounded ones become a loop. Mutual or
non-tail recursion, non-byte terminals such as `Token(...)`, annotated
rules (lookahead, `max_tokens`, capture, lazy, temperature, suffix stop)
and exceeding `max_num_states` return an error instead of a wrong
automaton.

consumer.

perf: make token masks under max_chars independent of the generated (#913)

A grammar with a single `max_chars` rule made every
`fill_next_token_bitmask` call cost O(generated length), and slowed the
masks of rules that are never under a budget.

Measured on a 30-property JSON schema grammar where only the `response`
string carries `max_chars=256` (Llama-3-8B tokenizer, 8 threads), mask
latency by length of the already generated prefix:

| prefix | no budget: response / other string | before: response / other
string | after: response / other string |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 chars | 140 / 133 µs | 1041 / 221 µs | 156 / 138 µs |
| 530 chars | 144 / 132 µs | 1846 / 304 µs | 156 / 139 µs |
| 2030 chars | 144 / 132 µs | 4272 / 541 µs | 156 / 139 µs |
| 8030 chars | 144 / 133 µs | 13197 / 1419 µs | 154 / 138 µs |

## Cause

When the byte-level walk rejects an uncertain token, the mask filler
retries it through the atomic token path, since a `Token`/`ExcludeToken`
edge may still accept it. That retry ran on a copy of the whole matcher
(`Impl atomic_trial(...)`), created once per state with uncertain tokens
and again for every rejected token. The copy includes every history row,
so each mask cost O(history) per rejected token, for every state of the
grammar. The JSON-schema grammar has no token edges, so all of it was
wasted.

## Change

Retry in place instead of on a copy: drop the rows of the partially
matched previous token, rebuild the single-state row, run the atomic
token path, then rebuild the row once more so enforcement performed by
the trial cannot leak into later tokens. The LCP shortcut is reset after
a retry. Skip the retry entirely when the grammar has no
`Token`/`ExcludeToken` edges (`has_token_edges_`, computed once from the
complete FSM), and use the precomputed per-token character counts
instead of recounting bytes.

The per-byte budget check (`AdvanceWithCharacterBudget`) is kept for
every state, since a token can finish an unbudgeted rule and continue
through the parent into a budgeted sibling; the scan it adds per
codepoint is negligible. The compile-time gates keyed on
`has_char_budget_rules_` (speculative masks, rule-level cache,
token-edge demotion) are unchanged and remain a follow-up.

## Validation

- Masks are unchanged: per-position bitmasks are identical between the
old and new implementation on nine grammars (budgeted
`TagDispatch(excludes=...)` inside JSON and as a raw body, `Token` edges
plus `max_chars`, `capture` plus `max_chars`, nested budgets, a rule
shared inside and outside a budget, two budgets) over Llama-3
tokenizations and a small vocabulary, with prefixes up to 3000
characters.
- Three new tests in `tests/python/test_max_chars.py`: the token-edge
retry under a budget, an unbudgeted rule keeping budget-free masks after
a long prefix, and a token that crosses from an unbudgeted rule into a
budgeted sibling (mask and `accept_token` must agree). All pass on
`main` too.
- `xgrammar_test` 82/82. Full `tests/python` with `HF_TOKEN`: 4854
passed, 3 skipped, 0 failed.
- Grammars without character budgets are unaffected: compile and mask
A/B against `main` is within noise.

Found while evaluating `TagDispatch(excludes=...)` with `max_chars` as a
cheaper representation for `JSONSchemaFormat.excludes` with `maxLength`
(#901).

feat: support string exclusions in JSON schema structural tags (#912)

feat: support string exclusions in JSON schema structural tags

Extracted from #901 by @izhuhaoran, fourth piece after #906, #909 and
#910. The branch keeps the original commit and its revert at the bottom
for attribution; the net diff against `main` is the `feat: support
string exclusions in JSON schema structural tags` commit plus `feat:
drop string length constraints when exclusions are present`, a refactor
of the exclusion helpers, and `feat: apply exclusions only to strings
without pattern or format`. The Kimi-K3 builtin wiring that turns this
on by default is the last piece and comes separately.

## Motivation

Kimi-K3 tool arguments are raw text. The model can emit control markers
such as `<|close|>response<|sep|>` inside an argument that is still
open, then start another tools/call block. The schema grammar accepts
all of that as string content, while the tool-call parser reads it as
structure. There is no way today to tell the converter that certain
substrings must never appear inside a string value.

## API

`JSONSchemaFormat` gets an optional `excludes: list[str]` (C++, Python,
TypeScript, docs):

```python
JSONSchemaFormat(json_schema=..., style="kimi_k3_xml", excludes=["<|open|>", "<|close|>", "<|sep|>"])
```

- Forbids each substring in string values and property names, including
nested JSON strings. It applies to the strings without `pattern` or
`format`: a `pattern` or `format` is the schema's own contract for the
string and is matched as is. Filtering those would intersect an
arbitrary regex with the exclusion automaton, which reproduces the
length blowup below for any pattern with a wide repetition
(`^[\s\S]{0,256}$` gives 4592 rules).
- `minLength`/`maxLength` are dropped when exclusions are set, with a
warning naming the string and the bounds. Bounding a filtered string's
length would multiply the grammar by the bound: one rule per position
and exclusion state, about 18 rules per character for the three Kimi-K3
markers, which is 18 s and 111 MiB for `maxLength: 256` and 110 s for
ten `maxLength: 128` properties. Without the bounds those schemas
compile in 96 ms and 71 ms, as the unbounded strings do.
- Matches the emitted text before JSON/XML unescaping, may span tokens,
and never spans separate strings. JSON delimiter quotes, numbers,
punctuation and XML parameter wrappers are outside the scope, so
`<|close|>` can still begin a valid `<|close|>argument<|sep|>`
terminator.
- `const`/`enum` alternatives and fixed property names that contain an
excluded substring are dropped; a required one makes the schema
unsatisfiable rather than silently allowed.
- An omitted or empty list changes nothing: every exclusion code path is
behind `!excludes_.empty()`.
- Errors instead of silent bypass: XML styles reject exclusions that
start or end with formatting whitespace, and `cohere_xml` and
`minimax_m3_xml` reject non-empty exclusions.

## Implementation

`ExcludingString` builds the FSM of the converter's own string body (the
JSON string content with escapes, or the XML identifier), intersects it
with the complement automaton of the excluded substrings (`Intersect`
with the budgets from #906), prunes states that can no longer reach an
accepting state so no dead-end prefix is ever offered in a mask, and
re-emits the result as EBNF rules with codepoint transitions. UTF-8 byte
paths are collapsed back to codepoint classes and never turned into a
second transition for an ASCII character, which relies on the canonical
encodings from #909. The closing JSON quote is appended after the
intersection because it is syntax, not content. Property names go
through the same intersection for `additionalProperties` keys and
through a substring check for fixed keys; keys constrained by
`patternProperties`/`propertyNames` patterns are matched as is like
patterned values. A length-bounded string with exclusions uses the
shared string rule (json) or the raw `TagDispatch` body (XML styles)
instead of an intersected length bound.

## Validation

- `tests/python/test_json_schema_excludes.py`: 91 cases covering every
style, nested JSON, property names and literals, Unicode and overlapping
exclusions, emitted-text semantics, patterned and formatted strings left
unfiltered, dropped length bounds and their warning, whitespace-boundary
and unsupported-style errors, compiler cache isolation, and token-mask
replays that reject the original Kimi-K3 bad output at `response` while
accepting the repaired output and a valid argument end.
- `xgrammar_test` 82/82. Full `tests/python` with `HF_TOKEN`: 4947
passed, 3 skipped; the two CUDA kernel tests that JIT-build a torch
extension fail identically on `main` in this environment (CUDA 11.1
toolkit).
- Rebased onto `main` after #908: the DeepSeek key exclusion check now
applies to both `deepseek_xml` and `deepseek_v4_1_xml`, which share the
raw-key path.
